contributions: Systematic review of 20 prerequisite concepts spanning linear algebra (dot product, matrix multiplication, eigenvalue decomposition, SVD), calculus (gradient descent, chain rule, backpropagation), and programming (PyTorch tensors, autograd, PyG, NetworkX)
Explicit connections between foundational math and GNN operations, e.g., showing that A@x is message passing and that eigenvectors of the Laplacian encode community structure
limitations: No prerequisites are required, but the chapter assumes comfort with undergraduate linear algebra and multivariable calculus; readers may need to skim or skip sections. It does not cover supervised learning or optimization fundamentals in depth, directing readers to a separate Machine Learning Textbook for that background.
methods: The chapter presents formal definitions, geometric intuition, and worked examples for each concept. It derives backpropagation for a two-layer network using the chain rule, shows PyTorch code for tensors and autograd, and demonstrates eigendecomposition and a complete training loop with Adam optimizer on a synthetic dataset.
results: No empirical results; the chapter is purely foundational. Key conceptual results include: cosine similarity formula sim(u,v) = (u·v)/(||u|| ||v||); the graph convolution connection where A@x sums neighbor features; the Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem for low-rank SVD approximation; Adam update rules with beta_1=0.9, beta_2=0.999, epsilon=1e-8; and a demonstration that autograd correctly computes dy/dx = 3x^2 - 2 = 10 at x=2.
tldr: This chapter builds the mathematical and computational foundation—linear algebra, calculus, backpropagation, and PyTorch—including the core tools needed to implement every GNN architecture in the textbook from scratch.
